title: Affine-segment preservation on a quarter ball

content.display_title: Affine-segment preservation on a quarter ball
content.one_sentence_role: Passes from midpoint preservation to every real parameter in a segment.
content.natural_language_statement: Let $E,F$ be real normed spaces, $f:S\to T$ a bijective isometry between subsets, and $c\in S$. Assume $R>0$, $B(c,R)\subseteq S$ and $B(f(c),R)\subseteq T$. For $x,y\in S\cap B(c,R/4)$ and $a\in[0,1]$, $$f((1-a)x+ay)=(1-a)f(x)+af(y).$$
content.assumptions: Both radius-$R$ open balls are contained in their respective sets. Both endpoints lie in the source quarter ball. The parameter is restricted to $0\le a\le1$.
content.conclusion: The same isometry preserves every point of the segment between these endpoints, with the same parameter $a$.
content.proof_summary: On the convex quarter ball, midpoint preservation gives an arithmetic progression at rational subdivision points. Continuity then gives all real parameters in the interval.
proof_steps: Put $U=B(c,R/4)$. If $x,y\in U$ and $0\le a\le1$, then $$\begin{aligned}\|(1-a)x+ay-c\|&\le(1-a)\|x-c\|+a\|y-c\|\\&<(1-a)\frac R4+a\frac R4=\frac R4.\end{aligned}$$ Hence $(1-a)x+ay\in U\subseteq S$. Restrict $f$ to $g:U\to F$. By [Quarter-ball midpoint theorem](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Normed/Affine/IsometryExtension/Local.lean#L137-L192), $g((z+w)/2)=(g(z)+g(w))/2$ for all $z,w\in U$.

Fix $n\ge1$ and set $$z_k=\left(1-\frac{k}{n}\right)x+\frac{k}{n}y,\qquad w_k=g(z_k)\quad(0\le k\le n).$$ Step 1 puts every $z_k$ in $U$. Since $z_k=(z_{k-1}+z_{k+1})/2$, midpoint preservation gives $$2w_k=w_{k-1}+w_{k+1},\qquad w_{k+1}-w_k=w_k-w_{k-1}.$$ Thus the successive differences are constant.

Summing the constant differences and using $w_0=g(x)$, $w_n=g(y)$ gives $$w_k=\left(1-\frac{k}{n}\right)g(x)+\frac{k}{n}g(y).$$ This proves the desired formula for every rational parameter in $[0,1]$.

For real $a\in[0,1]$, choose rationals $a_j\to a$. The isometry is continuous, and $$\|g((1-a_j)x+a_jy)-g((1-a)x+ay)\|=|a_j-a|\,\|y-x\|\longrightarrow0.$$ The affine combination on the right is continuous as well, so the rational identity passes to the limit. Replacing $g$ by the restriction of $f$ proves the theorem.
